title: Death Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: Death upright: endings, transformation; reversed: resisting change. Love, work, advice, Waite's 1911 text and the 1909 card. Draw it for your question.
image_alt: Death, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a rider in black armor on a white horse carries a black banner with a white rose; figures kneel before him and the sun shines between two towers.
capsule: Death is card XIII of the Major Arcana: endings, transformation and the release of a chapter that has run its course. Reversed, it shows a change you keep holding off. It is not a card to fear; its only caution is against clinging. Asked yes or no, upright it answers no, because something is finishing, not continuing.

blocks.heading: What is on the Death card?
paragraphs: A rider in black armor sits on a white horse and holds up a black banner with a large white rose. Waite writes that the horseman "moves slowly" and that the rose on the banner "signifies life" (p. 120). He adds that "the horseman carries no visible weapon" (p. 120).

On the 1909 card the rider's face is a bare skull under a helmet with a red plume, and XIII is printed on the banner; banner and rose are the largest shapes in the picture. In front of the horse a king lies on the ground with his crown beside him, a child holds out a few flowers, a young woman kneels with her head turned away, and a churchman in a yellow robe and mitre stands with joined hands. Waite names the same four: king, child, maiden and "a prelate with clasped hands" (p. 120).

Far behind them a boat sails on a river, and the sun stands between two towers on the horizon. Waite's line for it: "Between two pillars on the verge of the horizon there shines the sun of immortality" (p. 120).

Older decks showed a figure with a scythe. Waite set aside "the crude notion of the reaping skeleton" and wrote that the card speaks of "change, transformation and passage from lower to higher" (p. 120).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about Death?
paragraphs: In plain words, the first list is about things wearing out and reaching their end. Waite's full entry also gives separate readings for a man, a woman and a maid (p. 285), a fortune-telling habit of his time that Arcana Diary does not follow. The second list is quieter: inertia, sleep, lethargy, a life that stops moving.

Waite found the older occult readings of the thirteenth card "on the whole, better than usual" and named them: "rebirth, creation, destination, renewal" (p. 123). Surveying older decks, he also noted that "the alternatives allocated to the symbol are change and transformation" (pp. 23–24).

blocks.heading: What does Death mean upright?
paragraphs: Upright, Death points to endings that make room: a job, a role, a habit, a way of seeing yourself, a phase of a relationship that has done its work. The card names a transition, the stretch between what is finishing and what has not started yet. That stretch can feel strange or sad, and the card does not ask you to pretend otherwise.

Its point is transformation rather than loss. The rider's banner carries the rose that Waite reads as life, and on the horizon the sun is shining. Release is part of the meaning too: letting go of what has run its course, ideally with some thanks for what it gave you, is what clears the ground for the next stage.
If this fits your situation, the card's question is a quiet one: what in your life has already ended, even if you have not said so out loud?

blocks.heading: What does Death mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, Death usually describes resisting change: holding on to something that has already run its course, because the familiar feels safer than the unknown. The ending still moves forward, only slower, and you may feel stuck between phases, no longer in the old one and not yet in the new.
Waite's reversed list, with inertia, sleep and lethargy, is close to this reading: a standstill, life on pause. The reluctance to let go that sits behind it is a modern reading, not Waite's.

This side of the card is not a bad sign either. Ask what you are protecting by keeping things as they are, then release one small piece on purpose: an object, a routine, a commitment you no longer believe in.

blocks.heading: What does Death mean in love?
paragraphs: In love, Death speaks of change inside your own feelings and patterns. If you are single, it can point to closing the door on an old story: a past relationship you still measure everyone against, or a way of dating that no longer suits you. Clearing it out gives something more honest room to grow.

In a relationship, the card can describe a phase ending: roles, routines or expectations the two of you have outgrown. It does not decide whether a relationship goes on; it describes what is changing on your side.
Reversed in love, look at what you keep carrying: a hope, a habit, an old argument. Which of these could you set down?

blocks.heading: What does Death mean for work and money?
paragraphs: At work, Death can mark the end of a role, a project or a way of working that has given what it had to give. Its question is practical: what are you still doing only out of habit, and what would change if you stopped?
With money, look at your own patterns: which spending or saving habit belongs to a chapter you have already left?
Reversed, notice a work change you keep postponing even though you have outgrown the place you are in.

blocks.heading: What is Death's advice?
paragraphs: Clear out one object or habit that belongs to a chapter you are ready to close. Do it deliberately, as a small ritual: name what it gave you, then let it go. The advice of this card is not to force big endings, only to stop feeding what is already finished.

blocks.heading: Is Death a yes or no card?
Death as a person and as a feeling
paragraphs: When Death turns up to describe someone in a spread, it usually shows a person in the middle of a big change, closing one chapter before the next is clear. If it points at you, it marks the part of you that already knows something is over. The emotion behind it is a quiet mix of sadness and relief; reversed, it becomes reluctance, the wish to keep everything as it was.

pairs.text: After the ending comes quiet hope. Let the space that opened stay empty for a while before you fill it.
A goodbye you choose. You are the one walking away from what no longer satisfies.
A chapter closes and a clear call follows. Listen to what is asking for your attention next.
Something ends and a practical opening appears. Plant the new seed in the ground that was cleared.

blocks.heading: Death or The Tower?
paragraphs: Both cards are about endings, and they are often mixed up. Waite calls The Tower "The Tower struck by Lightning" (p. 25) and allows that it may also signify "the end of a dispensation" (p. 135). It is the sudden card: a shake-up from outside that clears away what was built on weak ground. Death is the slow one; its rider moves at a walk (p. 120). It is a chapter closing in its own time, something you can see approaching and prepare for.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about Death
paragraphs: What am I still carrying from a chapter that is already over?
What would I make room for if I let one old habit go?
Which ending in my life deserves a proper goodbye?

faq.q: Is the Death card good or bad?
faq.a: Neither, in the way the question is usually meant. Its name makes it one of the most misunderstood cards. In a reading it marks change and release, often uncomfortable and often useful. What it pushes against is staying in a phase after it has stopped giving you anything.

faq.q: Should the Death card be taken literally?
faq.a: No. The name is old and the picture is symbolic: Arcana Diary reads it as a chapter of your life closing, never as a forecast about anyone's life. Waite himself listed rebirth and renewal among its better readings (p. 123), and he replaced the scythe of older decks with a slow rider and a shining sun.

faq.q: Can the Death card be positive?
faq.a: Yes, often. Once people know what it means, many feel relief when it appears: permission to finish something that has dragged on too long. Next to hopeful cards in a spread, it reads as a clean break that frees the road. The hard part is usually the letting go, not what comes after.

faq.q: Is Death the saddest card in tarot?
faq.a: Not really. Change can carry sadness, but the card itself is calm: no weapon, a steady horse, a rose for a sign. Cards that put grief at the center, such as the Three of Swords, sit much closer to sorrow. Death is more about what is ending than about how much it hurts.

waite.quote: End, mortality, destruction, corruption … Reversed: Inertia, sleep, lethargy, petrifaction, somnambulism; hope destroyed.
